summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to plan and organise the work of a welding and fabrication team. You will set priorities, share out and delegate work by skill, work out the team's capacity and schedule the week, control stores and shared equipment, organise the workshop with 5S, communicate through briefings, handovers and job boards, and keep records. You will also monitor progress, solve problems, handle change and review the work so that each week runs better than the last.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). A skilled welder who becomes a team leader soon finds that the hard part is not the welding: it is getting the right people, materials, machines and information to the right job at the right time, safely, and keeping customers and the supervisor informed. This unit is about that work.

The methods here are used in every well-run workshop, from a two-person gate shop to a large fabrication yard: a priority list, a skills matrix, a capacity check, a schedule, a job board, a stores routine, 5S, short briefings and a weekly review.
**Who it is for:** Welding Level 3 trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and welders and fitters who lead, or will soon lead, a small team.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Sort jobs and tasks by how urgent and how important they are, with safety first, and agree the order with the supervisor.
Match tasks to people's skills and qualifications, delegate clearly, follow up, and develop the team.
Work out the productive hours the team really has, compare them with the work booked, and schedule the week.
Keep consumables in stock without overstocking, book shared machines, report breakdowns.
Lay out work to flow one way; use 5S and visual controls; deal with waste properly.
Brief the team, hand over clearly, work with other trades, keep customers informed, keep job sheets.
Track progress and key measures, act early when a job falls behind, find root causes, manage change.
Hold short reviews, record lessons learned and make small improvements every week.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on priorities, sharing and delegating work, capacity, scheduling, layout, 5S, stores, resources, time management, communication, workplace rules, safety in planning, monitoring, problem solving, change, teamwork, records, continuous improvement and waste.
A **written paper** with short answers (terms and simple calculations such as capacity, reorder levels and percentages) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Two team practicals**: organising a cluttered bay or store with 5S and setting up a visual job board; and planning a team's week (priorities, capacity, schedule, equipment bookings, stock orders, a note on any shortfall), then briefing the team and handling a customer's call about a late job.

blocks.note: Many short answers are worked from simple sums: hours × people × days, percentages, and reorder levels. Write the sum out in full each time, with its units, and check that the answer makes sense.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Planning the work: priorities and safety

blocks.p: Before you can plan, you need the facts for every job: what is to be made (drawing and job card), the estimated hours by task, the materials and consumables, the machines needed, the skills or qualifications needed, the due date and how firm it is, the customer, and the hazards.

**Urgent** means it must be done soon. **Important** means it carries real value or harm: safety, a customer's firm deadline, money, the Centre's reputation. Sort every job and task into one of four boxes.

head: Importance
Urgent
Not urgent
rows: A safety defect; a breakdown that stops other work; a paid job due tomorrow
A contract due in two weeks; planned maintenance; training a new member
Many phone requests; routine stock checks; small favours
Tidying old files during a busy week; jobs nobody has asked for

ul: **Safety comes before money.** Anything that could hurt someone is made safe at once (closed off, tagged out, guarded), and then the full repair is planned like any other job.
Important work that is not yet urgent gets a fixed date in the plan, so it does not turn into an emergency.
When two customers both want to be 'first', check the dates actually agreed and the priorities set by the supervisor, then confirm the plan with both customers. The loudest caller does not decide.

blocks.p: It is easier and cheaper to control a hazard at the planning stage than on the day. When you plan a job, plan its safety with it:

ul: Which hazards it brings (hot work, lifting, work at height, confined spaces, noise, fumes) and the controls, PPE and permits needed.
Which jobs must be kept apart: hot work and painting or solvent use; grinding next to a walkway; lifting over people.
The equipment needed for safety (extraction, screens, lifting gear, fire extinguishers) and that it is booked and working.
Who is trained and fit for each task; never plan a trainee onto work they are not ready for.
Hours: do not plan more overtime or longer shifts than the Centre's rules and the law allow. Tired people make mistakes.

blocks.note: Afternoons in a Jamaican workshop can be very hot. Plan the heaviest welding and grinding for the cooler morning, give water and rest breaks in the shade, and let new workers build up to full days in the heat. In the hurricane season (1 June to 30 November), keep a plan for securing loose sheet and steel, protecting machines and stock, and moving site dates when a storm is forecast.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: People: skills, sharing work and delegating

blocks.p: A **skills matrix** is a table of what each team member can do and how well. It shows at a glance who can do a task, who needs supervision, and where the team has gaps.

Key: 0 = not trained; 1 = under supervision; 2 = works alone to standard; 3 = can train others. A welder's qualification (for example for a process and position such as 6G pipe) is a fact, not a level: only a qualified welder does work that needs that qualification.

ul: Break each job into tasks and note any that need a qualification or a particular skill.
Match qualified and skilled people to the tasks that need them.
Pair a newer member with someone who can train others, so skills grow; a trainee works under supervision, never alone on work they are not ready for.
Keep the load fair and everyone busy; plan the order of tasks so nobody is left waiting for someone else.
Update the matrix as people gain skills, and plan training to fill the gaps.

blocks.p: A team leader who does every important task personally has no time left to plan, check and support the team, and the team learns less. **Delegating** means giving a task, and the authority to do it, to someone else, while you stay responsible for the result.

flow: Choose the right person for the task
Explain what is to be done, to which drawing and standard, and by when
Give the safety points, and make sure they have the tools, materials and information
Agree when they will report back, and what they can decide for themselves
Check that they understand: ask them to explain it back
Follow up at the agreed times; help, give feedback, and record the work

ul: Praise good work specifically and in front of others if they are comfortable with that.
Raise problems **privately**, early, calmly and with facts: what you saw, why it matters, what needs to change.
Agree the next step together, and check back later.
The Centre's or employer's **policies** (from HR or the manager) set the rules on hours, overtime, leave, lateness and reporting sick. Follow them, and the law, when you plan.
A **job description** lists the duties of each role; a **rota** shows who works which days and hours.
Shift swaps and leave are approved only when the work is covered and the rules are followed.
Overtime is usually paid at a higher rate, such as 1.5 times the normal rate, so it costs more and is planned, not assumed.

flow: Day one: induction: tour, emergency exits, first aid, the Centre's rules, PPE issue, a safety briefing
Introduce the team and give them a buddy, an experienced member who guides them
Find out what they can already do and put it on the skills matrix
First weeks: simple tasks under supervision, with clear instructions and checks
Move on to harder tasks as they show they are ready; practise on test pieces before customer work
Check progress and give feedback often; record the training given

blocks.p: When two members disagree (for example over a machine, a task or a shift), listen to each privately, get the facts, and agree a fair solution based on the needs of the work, such as a booking sheet for the machine. Do not take sides or ignore it; if it continues, involve the supervisor. Involving the team in planning the week reduces many disputes, because people support a plan they helped to make.

**Capacity** is the amount of work a team or machine can do in a set time. Plan with **productive hours**, not paid hours: each day some time goes on set-up, cleaning, briefings, breaks and moving between jobs.

Worked example: a team of 5 works 8-hour days for 5 days, which is 5 × 8 × 5 = 200 paid hours. Each person loses about 1.25 hours a day: 5 × 1.25 × 5 = 31.25 hours. One person is on leave for 2 days, losing another 2 × (8 − 1.25) = 13.5 productive hours. Capacity = 200 − 31.25 − 13.5 = **155.25 hours**.

Next, add up the estimated hours of every job booked for the week. If 170 hours are booked, the team is 14.75 hours short. Do not just hope the team works faster. Raise it with the supervisor early, with options:

ul: Overtime, within the Centre's rules and the law
Borrowing a worker from another team
Moving a job with a later or flexible date, after talking to its customer
Saving time, for example by batching cutting for several jobs
Subcontracting a task, if the supervisor agrees

blocks.h: How long will a task take?

blocks.p: Days = hours of work ÷ (number of people × productive hours each per day). 45 hours of fitting with 2 fitters at 6.5 productive hours each: 45 ÷ 13 = 3.5 days. Check that the work can really be split between the people (two fitters cannot always work on one small part).

head: Tool
What it shows
Good for
rows: Every job's stage at a glance, with its owner and due date
Daily control; everyone can see what is next
Each task as a bar against the days of the week, in order
Planning the week; seeing which tasks depend on others
Who has a shared machine or space, and when
Avoiding clashes over the plasma cutter, crane, paint booth
The leader's own tasks, with priorities marked

ul: **Dependencies:** some tasks cannot start until another finishes (painting after welding; welding after fit-up). Put them in order on the chart.

**Float** (spare time) is the number of days a job can slip without missing its date. A job needing 3 working days, which cannot start before Monday 7 December and is due on Thursday 10 December, has 4 working days available and **1 day of float**.
**Batching:** doing similar work together, such as cutting the plate for three jobs in one session, saves set-up time and lets offcuts be used better.
Keep a daily to-do list, mark the top priorities, and tick tasks off as they are done.
Block a short, fixed time for planning and paperwork, for example the first half hour of the day.
Break big tasks into steps with dates, and check progress daily.
When interrupted, ask: is this urgent? If yes, deal with it; if not, note it for a set time. Group calls and messages.
Stay easy to reach for safety problems and questions, and walk round the workshop regularly: supporting the team is part of the job, not an interruption.
At the end of the day, review the list and carry forward what is not done.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The list of everything held in the store, with quantities
A record for one item of what comes in, what goes out and what is left
How long an order takes to arrive
Extra stock always kept in reserve, in case a delivery is late or use is high
The stock level at which more is ordered, so it arrives before the safety stock is used
The most you hold, so money and space are not tied up and stock does not age
Older stock is used before newer stock, so nothing ages, rusts or gets damp on the shelf

blocks.p: **Reorder point = daily use × lead time (in days) + safety stock.** Example: cutting discs used at 25 a day, a 4-day lead time and a safety stock of 25: 25 × 4 + 25 = **125 discs**. If the lead time or the daily use changes, the reorder point must change too.
Ordering for a period: discs for 12 working days at 25 a day is 300 discs; in boxes of 50 that is 6 boxes. Always round up to whole boxes.

ul: Count stock regularly and compare it with the cards. A difference means stock is being used without being recorded, or has been lost or damaged: find the cause and fix the routine.

Store items correctly: electrodes dry, opened low-hydrogen electrodes in the holding oven, wire in its sealed packing, gas cylinders upright and chained, and oxygen kept apart from fuel gases as the Centre's rules say.
Keep a small, labelled stock of everyday consumables at each bay, topped up from the main store, so welders do not walk to the store all day.
Keep a **booking sheet** or shared calendar for shared machines and spaces, so clashes are seen and settled before the day.
**Downtime** is time a machine cannot be used because it is broken or being serviced. Plan servicing for quiet times, and plan round it.
Report breakdowns at once, tag the machine out of use, and re-plan the work that needed it.

blocks.p: Work should flow **one way**: steel store → marking and cutting → fitting → welding → grinding and finishing → painting → dispatch. This cuts carrying and crossing paths, so it is faster and safer. Keep welding bays screened and ventilated, painting well away from hot work, walkways marked and clear, and gas cylinders stored safely. A **layout** plan drawn to scale shows where machines, benches and stores are, and helps you plan changes.

head: Step
What it means
In the workshop
rows: Red-tag broken tools, scrap and items not used; record and remove them
A marked place for everything, near where it is used
Shadow boards, labelled racks and bins, marked floor areas
Clean the area, and inspect while cleaning
Daily sweep; cleaning shows up leaks, damaged cables and loose guards
Written routines so everyone keeps it the same way
A one-page checklist and photos of how the bay should look
Regular checks or audits, and the leader setting the example

blocks.p: A **shadow board** has the outline of each tool painted where it hangs, so a missing tool is seen at once and every tool has its place.

ul: Sort waste as the Centre's rules say: scrap steel and offcuts for recycling, used discs and general waste in their bins, paint tins, thinners and oily rags as hazardous waste in closed metal containers.
Never burn or bury waste in the yard, or pour liquids down a drain.
Keep useful offcuts, labelled by size, in a rack for future jobs; scrap the rest.

blocks.p: A short briefing at the start of each day (sometimes called a toolbox talk) tells the team the day's priorities, who does what, the hazards and any changes, and gives them a chance to raise problems. Keep it short, at the job board, and finish by asking for questions.
When work passes to another shift or person, a written handover says what has been done, what is left, any hazards, faults and changes, and where things are, so work is not repeated or done wrongly.

Electricians, painters, masons and other contractors often work in or near your area. Agree times and areas with them in advance, so teams do not get in each other's way or create hazards for each other (for example painting near hot work, or grinding over people below).

ul: Keep customers informed of progress. If a job will be late, tell them **early and honestly**: the reason, the new date, and what is being done. Confirm it in writing.
Never promise a date you know cannot be met, and never blame the customer to cover a delay.
Tell the supervisor about problems as soon as you know: shortfalls, breakdowns, safety issues, late deliveries.

head: Record
What it shows
rows: What was done on each job, by whom, how long it took and what materials were used; signed
What came in, what was used, what is on order
What was checked, the results, and who checked it
What happened, so causes can be fixed
Servicing and repairs of each machine
Who is trained and qualified for what

blocks.note: Write records at the time, clearly, and sign them. A record written days later from memory is often wrong, and an unsigned one cannot be trusted.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **key performance indicator (KPI)** is a simple measure that shows whether the team is doing well. Choose a few that matter and track them every week.

head: KPI
How it is worked out
Example
rows: Jobs finished by their due date ÷ jobs finished × 100
Hours spent putting work right ÷ total hours worked × 100
Hours booked to jobs ÷ hours available × 100
A rise in near misses is a warning

ul: Walk round at set times; look at progress, quality and safety for yourself; talk to each person.
Compare the work done with the plan. If a 10-day job is 30% done after 4 days, at the same rate it will take 4 ÷ 0.3 = 13.3 days in all, so it is heading for about 3.3 days late.
Act as soon as a job starts to slip, not on the due date.

flow: Find out why: missing material, a breakdown, a skill gap, extra work, an absence
Act on the cause: move people or tasks, fix or work round the problem, arrange help or overtime within the rules
If the date cannot be met, tell the supervisor and the customer early, with a new date
Record what happened, so it can be prevented next time
Describe the problem clearly, with facts
Contain it: stop it getting worse (for example keep wrong parts apart)
Find the root cause: ask 'why?' until you reach something you can fix
Fix the cause, not only the symptom
Check that the fix worked
Change the routine so it does not happen again

blocks.p: **Asking 'why?'** Example: a batch was late. Why? The plasma cutter was down for a day. Why? The torch failed. Why? Worn parts had not been replaced. Why? Nobody was responsible for checking them. The root cause is the missing check, so the fix is a named person and a daily checklist, not just a new torch.

head: Common problem
Good response
rows: Keep it apart and labelled; tell the supplier and the supervisor; re-plan the work meanwhile; never use it 'to save time'
Check the skills matrix, share out the tasks, adjust the plan, tell anyone affected
Tag it out and report it; move work to other machines or re-order the tasks; book the repair
Stop that part; query in writing; work on other tasks while you wait

blocks.p: When the manager adds an urgent job mid-week, re-check the priorities, show the manager what the new job will push back, agree the new order, and tell the team and any customers affected. Do not drop everything else half-done, and do not quietly refuse. A plan is a tool to be changed sensibly, not a promise that nothing will change.

A short review with the team at the end of each week compares what was planned with what happened: jobs on time, hours used, rework, safety, materials and machines. The team says what went well and what got in the way. Pick one or two problems, agree an action with a person and a date, and check next week whether it worked. At the end of each job, write down the **lessons learned** so the next job goes better.

flow: Plan: decide what to change and what result you expect
Do: try the change, on a small scale first if you can
Check: compare the result with what you expected
Act: keep the change and make it standard, or adjust it and try again

blocks.p: **Efficiency** means getting the most work done with the least waste of time, people and materials. Lean working names eight common wastes.

head: Waste
Workshop example
rows: Carrying steel back and forth across the shop because of a poor layout
Too much stock tying up money and space, or ageing on the shelf
Welders walking to a far store for discs and rods many times a day
People or jobs standing idle for materials, a machine, a drawing or a decision
Making more parts than ordered, or making them long before they are needed
Grinding welds smooth where the drawing does not ask for it
Rework and scrap from wrong cuts, poor welds or misread drawings
Not asking the team for ideas; leaving a skilled member on simple work

blocks.p: A **standard operating procedure (SOP)** describes a routine task step by step, so everyone does it the same safe way: setting up the plasma cutter, changing a gas cylinder, closing the bay at night. Good SOPs are short, use photos, and are kept where the task is done.

ul: A labelled stock of discs and electrodes at each bay, topped up daily, ends the walks to the store.
A booking sheet and batched cutting end the queue for the plasma cutter.
A one-page checklist at each bay keeps the 5S standard after the clean-up day.
A first-off check before each batch cuts rework.

blocks.note: Small changes made week by week add up to a better-run workshop, and a team that suggests the changes keeps them going.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can sort jobs and tasks with the urgent–important matrix, with safety first.
I can plan the safety of a job at the planning stage, including heat and keeping trades apart.
I can use a skills matrix to share out work and plan training.
I can delegate a task clearly and follow it up.
I can give feedback and deal with a disagreement fairly.
I can plan a new team member's induction and first weeks.
I can follow the workplace rules on hours, overtime, leave and shift swaps.
I can work out a team's capacity and compare it with the work booked.
I can work out how many days a task will take, and the float on a job.
I can use a job board, a bar chart and a booking sheet.
I can manage my own time and interruptions.
I can work out a reorder point and an order quantity, and keep stock records.
I can organise a workshop layout and apply 5S.
I can deal with workshop waste properly.
I can run a daily briefing, write a handover note and work with other trades.
I can tell a customer honestly about a delay.
I can keep job sheets and other records.
I can track KPIs and act when a job falls behind.
I can find the root cause of a problem and manage a change to the plan.
I can run a weekly review and name the eight wastes.

terms: 5S
Sort, set in order, shine, standardise, sustain: a method for organising a workplace
Capacity
The amount of work a team or machine can do in a set time
Delegation
Giving a task and the authority to do it to someone else, while staying responsible for it
Downtime
Time a machine cannot be used because it is broken or being serviced
Efficiency
Getting the most work done with the least waste of time, people and materials
First in, first out (FIFO)
Using older stock before newer stock
Float
The time a job can slip without missing its due date
Gantt (bar) chart
A chart showing each task as a bar against time
Inventory
The list of all items held in the store, with their quantities
Job board
A board showing every job's stage, owner and due date
Job description
A document listing the duties of a job role
Key performance indicator (KPI)
A simple measure of how well the team is doing
Lead time
How long an order takes to arrive
Lessons learned
Points written down at the end of a job so the next one goes better
Productive hours
Working hours left after set-up, cleaning, briefings and breaks
Reorder point
The stock level at which more is ordered
Root cause
The underlying reason a problem happened, which must be fixed to stop it recurring
Rota
A list showing who works which days and hours
Safety stock
Extra stock kept in reserve in case a delivery is late
Shadow board
A tool board with each tool's outline painted where it hangs
Skills matrix
A table of what each team member can do, and how well
Standard operating procedure (SOP)
Written steps for doing a routine task the same safe way every time
Urgent–important matrix
A grid for sorting tasks by how urgent and how important they are

c1.title: A crowded week in Mandeville
c1.text: Sheldon leads a team of five at a fabrication shop in Mandeville, Manchester. Each person works 8-hour days, Monday to Friday, and loses about 1.5 hours a day to set-up, cleaning and breaks; one welder is on approved leave on Thursday and Friday. The jobs booked need 175 hours: hotel handrails due this Friday, a school gate due next Wednesday, and a trailer repair whose owner phones every day but has no agreed date. On Monday morning a trainee reports that the guard on the band saw is cracked.

c2.title: Stores and bookings in St Ann's Bay
c2.text: Karlene runs the welding stores at a training centre in St Ann's Bay, St Ann. Grinding discs are used at about 30 a day; until now a delivery took 3 working days and the safety stock was 30 discs. The supplier has told her deliveries will now take 5 working days. Her stock card for discs shows 140, but she counts only 95 on the shelf. Two classes both want the plasma cutter on Wednesday morning.

c3.title: A late staircase in Old Harbour
c3.text: Everton's team in Old Harbour, St Catherine, is making a steel staircase that was planned to take 6 working days. After 3 days it is only 40% done, mainly because the plasma cutter was out of action for a day. The team found that its torch failed because worn parts had not been replaced, and that nobody was responsible for checking them.

c4.title: Developing the team in Claremont
c4.text: Juliet leads a team in a shop in Claremont, St Ann. On the skills matrix, Lascelles is at level 3 (can train others) on the plasma cutter, and Orville is at level 1 (under supervision). Next week's job needs 60 brackets cut on the plasma cutter. Juliet has also delegated the fit-up of a gate to Orville, due Friday, and has noticed that his tack welds this week have been poorly placed.

c5.title: A 5S day in Highgate
c5.text: Winston's team spends a day applying 5S to a cluttered bay at a workshop in Highgate, St Mary. They find broken clamps, an old grinder that no longer works, and offcuts nobody has used for a year. Three weeks after the clean-up, the bay is cluttered again.

questions.q: What is the team's capacity in productive hours this week?
o: 162.5 hours
146.5 hours
149.5 hours
184.0 hours
questions.why: Paid hours are 5 × 8 × 5 = 200; set-up and breaks take 5 × 1.5 × 5 = 37.5, leaving 162.5. The two days of leave remove 2 × 6.5 = 13 more productive hours: 149.5. Taking off 16 hours for the leave counts the 1.5 hours a day twice.

questions.q: What should Sheldon do first about the band saw?
o: Take it out of use and tag it until the guard is replaced
Let it be used carefully until the handrails are finished
Put it on the list to look at after the school gate is done
Ask the trainee to tape the crack so work can carry on
questions.why: A damaged guard is both urgent and important: someone could be hurt today. Make it safe at once (out of use and tagged), then plan the repair and re-plan the cutting round it.

questions.q: The work is about 25 hours more than the capacity. Which plan is best?
o: Move the handrails to next week, as hotel jobs can always wait a bit
Do the trailer first, since its owner is the one who phones daily
Tell nobody and hope that the team works faster than usual
Agree a later date with the trailer owner; keep the others on time
questions.why: The handrails and gate have agreed dates; the trailer has none. Agreeing a date with its owner frees about the right number of hours. Phone calls do not set priorities, and the supervisor is told about the plan.

questions.q: By how much should Karlene raise the reorder point for discs?
o: By 90 discs
By 60 discs
By 30 discs
By 150 discs
questions.why: Reorder point = daily use × lead time + safety stock. Two more days of lead time at 30 discs a day add 60 discs: it rises from 120 to 180.

questions.q: What should Karlene do about the 45 missing discs?
o: Change the stock card to 95 and say nothing more about it
Recount, then find and fix how stock leaves unrecorded
Order 45 discs at once and leave the stock card as it is
Lock the store so that nobody can take discs at all
questions.why: A gap between the card and the shelf means stock is going out without being recorded, or being lost. Correct the card, but also find and fix the cause, or the gap will come back.

questions.q: How should the clash over the plasma cutter be settled?
o: Let whichever class reaches the cutter first on Wednesday use it
Cancel both classes' cutting until a second cutter is bought
Let the class with more trainees use it for the whole morning
Agree times on the booking sheet, and batch each class's cutting
questions.why: A shared booking sheet shows the clash before the day, and the instructors can agree times. Batching each class's cutting into one session saves set-up time for both.

questions.q: At the end of the day a half-used packet of low-hydrogen electrodes is found on a bench. What should the stores routine say?
o: Put them back in the holding oven, as the maker requires
Leave them on the bench, ready for the first job next morning
Put them back in the store's cupboard with the unopened packets
Throw them away, as an opened packet can never be used again
questions.why: Low-hydrogen electrodes take up moisture from the air, which leads to porosity and cracking. Once opened, they are kept in a holding oven as the maker and the Centre's procedure say.

questions.q: If the work carries on at the same rate, about how late will the staircase be?
o: About 3 days
About 4.5 days
About 1.5 days
About 0.5 days
questions.why: 40% in 3 days means the whole job takes 3 ÷ 0.4 = 7.5 days, against the 6 planned: about 1.5 days late. 4.5 days is the time still needed, not the delay.

questions.q: What should Everton do now?
o: Wait until the due date to see whether the team manages to catch up
Cut out the final inspection so that the job finishes on time
Tell the customer the delay was caused by the steel supplier
Act to recover time, and tell the supervisor and customer early
questions.why: Acting early gives the most options: moving people, overtime within the rules, or a new date agreed in good time. Skipping checks or giving a false reason damages quality and trust.

questions.q: Which action fixes the root cause of the cutter breakdown?
o: Buy a new torch, and then carry on using it exactly as before
Give one person the job of checking torch parts daily
Tell the team to handle the plasma cutter more gently from now on
Book the plasma cutter for fewer hours in each future week
questions.why: Asking 'why?' leads past the failed torch to the real cause: nobody checked the worn parts. A named person and a checklist stop it happening again; a new torch alone does not.

questions.q: Who should cut the 60 brackets, and how?
o: Lascelles leads, and Orville cuts some under his supervision
Orville cuts them all alone, so that he gains experience quickly
Juliet cuts them all herself, as she is responsible for the job
Lascelles cuts them all, and Orville sweeps the bay meanwhile
questions.why: A level 3 member can do the work to standard and train others. Pairing him with a level 1 member gets the job done well while Orville builds the skill, and the matrix is updated when he is ready.

questions.q: How should Juliet raise Orville's poorly placed tack welds with him?
o: At the next team meeting, so that everyone learns from his mistakes
At the end of the year, in his written review, with the other points
Privately and soon, showing examples and agreeing what will change
By re-doing his tack welds herself, so the gate is right, and saying nothing
questions.why: Feedback works best early, in private, based on facts, with a clear agreed next step and a check later. Doing it yourself in silence means he never improves.

questions.q: Juliet has delegated the gate fit-up to Orville. How should she follow it up?
o: Leave him alone until Friday so that he feels fully trusted
Stand beside him all week and check every tack he makes
Check at the agreed times against the drawing, and help
Ask the customer on Friday whether the finished gate is right
questions.why: Delegating does not end the leader's responsibility. Agreed check points let her catch problems early and support him, without taking the task back.

questions.q: In which 5S step are the broken clamps and the old grinder red-tagged?
o: Shine
Standardise
Set in order
Sort
questions.why: Sort means removing what is not needed. Red tags mark broken or unused items so they are recorded, decided on, and taken out of the bay.

questions.q: The bay is cluttered again three weeks later. Which 5S step was weak?
o: Sort
Sustain
Shine
Set in order
questions.why: Sustain keeps the standard going through regular checks, audits and example. Without it, a clean-up day is soon undone.

questions.q: Last month a team spent 18 hours on rework out of 240 hours worked. What was its rework rate?
questions.why: Rework rate = rework hours ÷ total hours × 100 = 18 ÷ 240 × 100 = 7.5%. Tracked month by month, a rising rate shows that quality problems need attention.

questions.q: A welder cuts and welds 40 brackets when the customer ordered 20, "to get ahead". Which of the eight wastes is this?
o: Over-production
Over-processing
Excess inventory
Motion
questions.why: Making more than was ordered, or making it before it is needed, is over-production. It uses time, steel and consumables that other jobs needed, and the extra brackets may never be sold.

questions.q: Welding a frame takes 3 days and starts on Monday. Painting takes 2 days and cannot start until welding is finished. What is the earliest day painting can finish?
o: Wednesday
Thursday
Friday
Monday of next week
questions.why: Welding runs Monday to Wednesday, so painting can only start on Thursday and finishes on Friday. Tasks that depend on each other are put in order on the bar chart.

questions.q: In the Plan, Do, Check, Act cycle, what happens at the 'Check' stage?
o: Check that every member of the team agrees with the change
Check the stock before any change at all can be tried out
Check the plan with the customer before it is put into action
Compare the result of the change with what was expected
questions.why: Check means measuring what the change actually did against the expected result. Act then keeps the change as the new standard, or adjusts it and tries again.

questions.q: A hurricane is forecast to reach Jamaica in two days. What should the team leader plan?
o: Carry on as normal, since forecasts often change and may well be wrong
Secure loose steel, protect machines and stock, and move site dates
Send the team home at once, leaving the yard and stock as they are
Rush all site work through before the storm, whatever the weather
questions.why: Loose sheet and steel become dangerous in high winds, and flooding can ruin machines and stock. Securing the shop and moving site work, with customers told, protects people and the business.
